query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially replacing the high-density hafnium (Hf) in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with additional low-density titanium (Ti) will reduce the overall density without significantly compromising its room-temperature and ~1000 °C mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g/cm³ exhibiting a single-phase BCC solid-solution structure and high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Reduce Hf content by substituting a portion of Hf with extra Ti (e.g., modifying the composition from HfMoTaTiZr to roughly Hf0.5MoTaTi1.5Zr).
generation.conditions: Tested under standard tensile and compressive loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase BCC microstructure with preserved lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening effects.
generation.mechanism: Hf is a heavy element that substantially contributes to the overall density. By partially substituting Hf with Ti—a lighter element that is still effective in maintaining the BCC structure and solid-solution strengthening—the average atomic mass is reduced while the key deformation mechanisms responsible for strength (such as dislocation movement within a distorted lattice) remain active.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to show a density reduction (potentially in the range of a 10–20% decrease) while retaining comparable yield strength and ductility at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: The original as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of 10.21 g/cm³ and demonstrated high mechanical performance at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to applications that require balanced mechanical performance at ambient conditions and at elevated temperatures (near 1000 °C) under typical tensile and compressive loads; the intervention must preserve the single-phase BCC structure.
generation.uncertainty: The exact balance between density reduction and potential minor losses in high-temperature strength is uncertain. Fine-tuning the substitution level is critical as excessive reduction in Hf might undermine key solid-solution strengthening contributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy variants under identical casting conditions: the standard HfMoTaTiZr alloy and the modified alloy with partial Hf replacement (e.g., Hf0.5MoTaTi1.5Zr). Conduct a suite of mechanical tests at room temperature and at ~1000 °C. Perform density measurements and microstructural analyses (using XRD and SEM) to confirm phase integrity.
measurements: Phase structure verification via X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy exhibits a reduction in yield strength or ductility greater than approximately 15% at room temperature or 1000 °C compared to the as-cast alloy, or if the BCC single-phase microstructure is lost, then the hypothesis is falsified.

After discussing the law of strength change with temperature and analyzing the results of the transmission electron microscopy, it is concluded that the deformation of the alloy at high temperature is mainly controlled by dislocation, and the morphology and density of the dislocation control the mechanical properties of the alloy. AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
